strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored and practically relevant problem: neural multi-objective routing on multigraphs, which as far as the related work indicates has not been tackled before with learning-based methods for combinatorial problems like TSP/VRP.

Two well-motivated architectural variants (edge-based GMS-EB and dual-head GMS-DH) offer a sensible trade-off between simplicity/accuracy and scalability/speed, and the design choices (hypernetwork preference conditioning, GREAT encoder, multi-pointer decoder, curriculum learning) are grounded in established techniques adapted thoughtfully to the multigraph setting.

Theoretical grounding via Proposition 1 clarifies when pruning is exact under linear scalarization, motivating why a learned selection mechanism is needed for more general cases (e.g., Chebyshev scalarization or nonlinear costs like time-windows).

Extensive experimental evaluation across many problem types (MOTSP, MOCVRP, MGMOTSP, MGMOTSPTW), distributions (EUC, TMAT, XASY, FIX, FLEX), instance sizes, and baselines (LKH, OR-tools, four MOEAs, a custom MatNet-based neural baseline), with substantial appendix material including ablations and zero-shot generalization to larger instances/more edges.

Informative ablation studies (GMS-DH vs. pre-pruning variant, learned vs. simple pruning) that isolate the contribution of the learned edge-selection mechanism, particularly showing its value in the more complex time-window setting.
Reports both solution quality (HV) and runtime, offering a fairly complete picture of the accuracy/speed trade-offs relative to strong non-learning baselines like LKH3.
weaknesses: Novelty is primarily architectural recombination of existing components (GREAT encoder, POMO, MatNet, multi-pointer decoder, hypernetwork conditioning) applied to a new problem setting, rather than fundamentally new algorithmic ideas; the core technical contribution is somewhat incremental.

All experiments rely on synthetic distributions (FIX/FLEX, TMAT/XASY) for multigraph edges; despite the paper's motivation citing real-world VRP cost savings from multigraph modeling, there is no evaluation on real or semi-realistic multigraph network data (e.g., actual road networks with alternative paths), leaving practical relevance somewhat unvalidated.

On the core MOTSP and MGMOTSP benchmarks, the proposed models do not outperform the strong classical heuristic LKH3 in solution quality (only closing most of the gap), so the main benefit is speed rather than better solutions; this weakens the 'competitive results' claim in some settings, especially as LKH is not really a learning baseline competitor in the traditional sense.

GMS-EB scales poorly (O(MN^4)) and has very high training times (e.g., 1.7h/epoch on multigraphs), which raises reproducibility/practicality concerns, particularly given 200 training epochs and multiple problem/distribution combinations evaluated.

The paper does not empirically compare against recently cited neural methods for asymmetric-graph MO routing (Santiyuda et al. 2024; Zhou, Kong, and Wang 2025), even in adapted/simplified form, which would have strengthened claims of relative performance.

The multigraph distributions considered (FIX2/FLEX2, occasionally FIX5/FLEX5) involve a small, fixed number of parallel edges, which may not capture the complexity or heterogeneity of real multigraph scenarios (e.g., many alternative routes with correlated attributes).

strengths: Addresses a novel and practically motivated problem (multi-objective routing on multigraphs) that has not been tackled by neural methods before, clearly differentiating this work from prior neural CO literature that assumes simple graphs.

Proposes two complementary architectures (GMS-EB and GMS-DH) with a clear trade-off between simplicity/accuracy and scalability, both built on a principled GNN encoder (GREAT) adapted for edge-permutation invariance in multigraphs.

Extensive empirical evaluation across many problem variants (MOTSP, MOCVRP, MGMOTSP, MGMOCVRP, MGMOTSPTW), distributions (EUC, TMAT, XASY, FLEX, FIX), instance sizes, and objective counts (bi- and tri-objective), with strong classical baselines (LKH, HGS, OR-tools) and multiple MOEAs.

Careful ablation studies (e.g., GMS-DH with pre-pruning vs. learned selection-decoder, and simplified pruning heuristic vs. learned pruning) that isolate the contribution of the proposed learned edge-selection mechanism, particularly convincing on the harder MGMOTSPTW problem.

Thoughtful theoretical grounding (Proposition 1) explaining when simple pruning suffices and motivating why learned pruning is needed in more general (e.g., nonlinear or Chebyshev-scalarized) settings.

Thorough appendix work, including additional naive neural baselines (GRBM, GOBM) that show the proposed method's robustness is not merely an artifact of using a particular baseline, plus zero-shot generalization experiments to larger sizes and more parallel edges.
weaknesses: GMS-EB has poor scaling (O(MN^4)) and very long training times (e.g., 1.7h/epoch on multigraphs per Table 4), which limits its practical applicability despite being presented as a core contribution.

The multigraph distributions (FLEXx, FIXx) are synthetic constructions for benchmarking purposes and do not obey the triangle inequality or reflect realistic transportation network structure; no experiments are conducted on real-world or more realistic multigraph instances (e.g., derived from actual road networks as in Ben Ticha et al.), leaving the practical relevance claims not fully substantiated empirically.

On several core problems (MOTSP, MGMOTSP, MGMOCVRP) the proposed neural methods do not outperform strong classical solvers like LKH/HGS/OR-tools, only closing part of the gap, which somewhat tempers the significance of the contribution relative to non-learning approaches, though this is a common characteristic of neural CO work.

Several architectural components (GREAT encoder, multi-pointer decoder, hypernetwork preference conditioning) are directly reused or lightly adapted from prior work, so the core novelty lies primarily in combining these pieces for the multigraph setting and in the selection-decoder design, which is a relatively incremental (albeit well-executed) contribution.

GMS-DH's zero-shot performance degrades noticeably for larger numbers of parallel edges (e.g., FIX10-100), suggesting the learned selection-decoder does not scale robustly with edge multiplicity, a limitation acknowledged but not deeply analyzed.

The paper's presentation relies heavily on extensive appendices (novelty justification, architecture details, extended related work) to substantiate claims made in the main text, suggesting the main paper alone may not fully convey the technical contribution and comparisons clearly.
